newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Pynzenyk promises to end corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Pynzenyk promises to end corruption.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Pynzenyk, blasting parliament for slowing reforms and government officials for feathering their nests, said on Saturday that Ukraine must eradicate corruption to boost foreign investment.
"The situation is crazy. In Ukraine the basis for economic growth is there but there is no growth," he said, bemoaning a fall in output last month of 10.4 percent year-on-year.
And Pynzenyk, seen alongside central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko as one of the former Soviet republic's strongest advocates of reforms, said he knew who was to blame.
"There is no growth because a lot of people are more interested in their own pockets...Not poor people, but government officials," he said.
Pynzenyk almost made clear that one of the main barriers to foreign investment was corruption at various levels.
For example, a rule which forces Ukrainian enterprises to obtain a licence before getting foreign investment would be scrapped if a law making its way through parliament were passed.
"I see no reason to license the receipt of such credits. Except one. Corruption," he said.
A new register of investors would also act as an incentive, Pynzenyk added.

President Leonid Kuchma, who sacked his agriculture minister and deputy transport minister at the first meeting of a new anti-corruption body this month, has often spoken of the need for staff changes in the ministries recently.

"I think the main issue is not the staffing one...But it is essential to have a group of people who can play the same tune. And that's always a problem for Ukraine," Pynzenyk said when asked if any more ministers would be sacked.

Interfax-Ukraine news agency said the work of the ministries of finance, economy, machine-building, military-industrial complex and statistics had been sharply criticised at a cabinet of ministers meeting on Friday.
It said the cabinet had asked Kuchma, on holiday in western Ukraine, to "strengthen the ministries."
The government's reform package, which has been passed at its first reading but could face several more readings in parliament, also foresaw stricter budget mechanisms.
Pynzenyk blamed parliament for the slow passage of a package of reforms, first presented in November.
The 1997 budget and the reforms must be approved before Ukraine can receive a new $2.5-$3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility credit from the International Monetary Fund.

Pynzenyk said "kartateka" -- where enterprises can legally avoid paying taxes by officially declaring they have no funds -- was one of the main reasons for a shadow economy estimated by experts at between 40 and 50 percent of output.

"They come one month and say I have no money, then another, and say they have no money, then another," Pynzenyk said, piling up sheets of paper on the table for each new registration to demonstrate his despair at the system. "And the tax authorities can do nothing about it."
Asked when he thought the conservative-dominated parliament would approve the laws, he replied: "What is more important is that they are passed."

He hinted that the government might offer social subsidies as a sop to conservatives in parliament to get the rest of the laws passed. "It is better to approve 25 percent of a law than not at all," he said.
